extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/practitioners (those using 37 CFR 1.132 SMEDs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance to USPTO examiners (and to applicants/practitioners) on use, admissibility, and evaluation of Subject Matter Eligibility Declarations (SMEDs) filed under 37 CFR 1.132 to address §101 rejections during patent prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary submission of SMED under 37 CFR 1.132
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants and practitioners may file Subject Matter Eligibility Declarations (SMEDs) under existing Rule 132 declaration practice; submission of a SMED is entirely optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo reminds applicants of the existing voluntary option, describes SMEDs as an underutilized path to proffer evidence to establish subject matter eligibility, and urges applicants who choose to file to submit a SMED separate from any other declarations (e.g., those addressing non-101 rejections). SMEDs can clarify the record and lead to stronger issued patents. This memorandum does not announce any new USPTO practice or procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements and timeliness (MPEP 716 / 37 CFR 1.132)
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration must be timely filed and comply with the formalities set forth in MPEP 716 and 37 CFR 1.132 to be entered and entitled to consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalities include timeliness (see MPEP 716.01), proper signature, inclusion of statutorily required language (e.g., recognizing penalties for willful false statements under 18 U.S.C. 1001), and other particulars in MPEP 716. If the examiner determines the declaration meets formal requirements, the examiner must consider it on the merits. Examiners should refer to MPEP 716 for handling declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may sign a declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who has knowledge of the facts being asserted may sign the declaration (inventor, inventor's co-worker, an independent expert, or others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No special qualification other than knowledge of the facts is required. An affidavit may be used in place of a declaration, but declarations are the typical vehicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement between claimed invention and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: For an evidentiary declaration to be relevant, there must be a nexus between the invention as claimed and the evidence provided in the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a SMED may demonstrate how one of ordinary skill in the art would interpret a specification that describes a technological improvement to show the claimed invention is patent-eligible; the examiner must determine whether the SMED improperly supplements the specification and whether a nexus exists before weighing the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence must be supported by actual proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To be of probative value, any objective evidence submitted in a SMED should be supported by actual proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable factual support can include expert testimony, objective comparative testing, trade articles, state-of-the-art documentation, and other objective evidence demonstrating improvements or factual bases. The declaration should present the underlying factual basis for any conclusions asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations cannot improperly supplement the original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration may not be used to supply information that was required to be present in the original disclosure upon filing (i.e., it cannot improperly supplement the specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, a declaration may be used to establish facts as of the filing date. When applicants know at filing that certain evidence would favor eligibility, they are strongly encouraged to include that evidence in the specification. Examiners should assess whether the SMED improperly supplements the specification in light of MPEP 716.09 and related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal conclusions vs factual bases
rubrics_metrics.description: An opinion as to the legal conclusion itself (e.g., that the claim is eligible or ineligible) is not entitled to weight, while the underlying factual basis for the opinion may be persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarants should provide factual evidence and the factual basis for expert conclusions (state of the art, test results, specific structural/operational details) rather than mere legal opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must weigh declaration with all record evidence under preponderance standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a declaration is properly presented, the examiner must weigh all relevant evidence of record and determine eligibility based on the preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declaration must be taken into account but will not necessarily control the eligibility determination. If the rejection is maintained or withdrawn in the next Office action, the examiner must explain, based on all evidence of record including the declaration, why the subject matter eligibility rejection has or has not been overcome. See MPEP 716.01(d) and MPEP 2106.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Document examiner findings and use prescribed form paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should document findings and conclusions in the next Office action after considering a SMED, and should use Form Paragraphs 7.65 or 7.66 to comment on the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the SMED overcomes the prima facie case of ineligibility, the Office action should explain why based on the totality of evidence; if not, the Office action should explain why the SMED failed to overcome the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: SMEDs can demonstrate how a claim is not a judicial exception or is integrated into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: A SMED may demonstrate that a claim does not recite a judicial exception, identify when a judicial exception is integrated into a practical application, or demonstrate that a claim amounts to significantly more than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual evidence (expert testimony, objective data, explanation of how claimed elements effect a practical application) to show integration into a practical application under Alice Step 2 (e.g., the additional elements apply/use the exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis). Examiners should evaluate nexus and non-supplementation before relying on these showings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of factual showings that can rebut Step 2 rejections (illustrative scenarios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific factual showings that may be persuasive under Alice Step 2 include: (a) evidence that claimed limitations cannot practically be performed in the human mind; (b) evidence the claim improves the functioning of a computer or another technology; (c) objective comparative testing showing superior performance of a claimed architecture; (d) evidence that claimed rules enable automation of tasks previously subjective to humans; (e) evidence that additional claim elements effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis; and (f) evidence that an unconventional arrangement of conventional elements provides technical advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo provides multiple hypotheticals illustrating each type (e.g., distributed network monitoring that cannot be done in the human mind; self-referential table improving storage and retrieval; neural network architecture with objective comparative testing; animation automation supported by trade articles; prophylaxis schedule adjustment that lowers disease risk; remote ISP filtering arrangement providing efficient operations). In each case, examiner must ensure no improper supplementation and a nexus exists before weighing the evidence under the preponderance standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desjardins precedent and what counts as 'something more' under Alice
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in computational performance, learning, storage, data sets and structures, and changes to system architecture (how information flows) can constitute patent-eligible technological advancements under the Alice framework when properly shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo cites the precedential ARP decision In re Desjardins and emphasizes that Section 101 remains a gatekeeper but must be applied properly; §§102/103/112 remain the proper inquiries for defining claim scope. When evaluating 'something more,' consider how the invention is applied, how it operates, and what it accomplished (architectural/system-level changes are particularly probative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training resources and internal materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Training resources on subject matter eligibility and declaration practice are available to examiners (35 U.S.C. 101 intranet page and specific Rule 132 training materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed resources include: Entry Level and TEE Training: Declaration Practice Under 37 CFR 1.132; TC 1600 Job Aid on Evidence of Unexpected Results Under 37 CFR 1.132; and Declaration practice under 37 CFR 1.132 (Rule 132). Examiners should consult these for handling SMEDs.
